source_refs.note: Exercise 4.2, Question 10: Inverse of A and A^{-1}A = I_3 (book page 60).

blocks.prompt: 10. Find the inverse of \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ -5 & 0 & 4 \\ 5 & 4 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) and show that \(A^{-1}A = I_3\).
blocks.explanation:
We must find the inverse of a \(3 \times 3\) matrix and then verify it.
Plan: all nine cofactors, \(|A|\), adjoint (transpose of the cofactor matrix), \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj}A\), then multiply \(A^{-1}A\).
steps:
Given: \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ -5 & 0 & 4 \\ 5 & 4 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\)
To find: \(A^{-1}\), and to show \(A^{-1}A = I_3\).
Method: \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj}A\), where \(\operatorname{adj}A\) is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors; it exists only if \(|A| \neq 0\).

\(|A|\) (expand along row 1)
\[|A| = 1(-16) + 2(20) + 1(-20)\]
\[= -16 + 40 - 20 = 4 \neq 0\]
Why: Row 1 entries times their cofactors. \(|A| \neq 0\), so \(A\) is non-singular and \(A^{-1}\) exists.

Adjoint (transpose of the cofactor matrix)
\[\operatorname{adj}A = \begin{bmatrix} -16 & 4 & 8 \\ 20 & -5 & -9 \\ -20 & 6 & 10 \end{bmatrix}\]
Why: The cofactors of row 1 \((-16, 20, -20)\) become column 1, and so on.

Inverse
\[A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix} -16 & 4 & 8 \\ 20 & -5 & -9 \\ -20 & 6 & 10 \end{bmatrix}\]
\[= \begin{bmatrix} -4 & 1 & 2 \\ 5 & -\frac{5}{4} & -\frac{9}{4} \\ -5 & \frac{3}{2} & \frac{5}{2} \end{bmatrix}\]
Why: Divide every entry of \(\operatorname{adj}A\) by \(|A| = 4\).

Divide by \(|A|\)
\[A^{-1}A = \dfrac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\]
\[= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = I_3\]
Why: \(A^{-1}A = \frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{adj}A)A\); the diagonal 4s become 1s.
